title: V445 Puppis: Galaxy's Only Helium Nova Fires 'Cosmic Bullets' at 30 Million km/h
excerpt: The unique stellar explosion, first detected in 2000, ejected high-speed knots of gas from a "vampire" white dwarf system 25,000 light-years away — and new research confirms it will never become a supernova.
body:
• V445 Puppis is the only known helium nova in the galaxy, producing a hydrogen-free explosion powered by a white dwarf devouring helium from its companion star.
  • Knots of ejected gas are hurtling through space at approximately 30 million km/h, with the expanding bipolar shell itself moving at 24 million km/h.
  • A December 2024 study by Bradley Schaefer at Louisiana State University conclusively shows the system will not become a Type Ia supernova, overturning years of speculation.
  • The research hinges on the Chandrasekhar limit — named after Indian-American Nobel laureate Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar — the mass threshold governing white dwarf explosions.

A binary star system 25,000 light-years from Earth is firing bullet-like knots of gas at roughly 30 million kilometres per hour — among the fastest ejecta ever observed from a nova. V445 Puppis, located in the constellation Puppis, is the only known helium nova in the Milky Way, and it continues to puzzle and fascinate astronomers more than two decades after it first erupted.

The system was first detected in November 2000, when it underwent a sudden outburst. What made it unprecedented was the total absence of hydrogen in its spectrum — a first for any observed nova. Instead, the explosion was dominated by helium, carbon, and other heavy elements, according to the European Southern Observatory (ESO).

A Vampire Star's Violent Feast

V445 Puppis is a binary system in which a dense, compact white dwarf — the remnant of a dead star — siphons helium-rich material from its companion, an evolved giant star that has been stripped of its outer hydrogen envelope. When enough helium accumulates on the white dwarf's surface, it ignites in a thermonuclear explosion: a helium nova.

"This is critical, as we know that Type Ia supernovae lack hydrogen, and the companion star in V445 Pup fits this nicely by also lacking hydrogen, instead dumping mainly helium gas onto the white dwarf."

— Danny Steeghs, University of Warwick

Using the NACO adaptive optics instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Chile, astronomers led by Patrick Woudt of the University of Cape Town captured time-lapse images of the expanding shell over two years. The images revealed a remarkable bipolar structure — an hourglass-shaped nebula with a narrow waist — unlike anything previously observed around a nova, according to ESO.

Two dense knots at the extreme ends of the shell were clocked moving at approximately 8,450 km/s, or about 30 million km/h. The shell itself was expanding at roughly 6,720 km/s, or 24 million km/h. A thick equatorial disc of dust, produced during the outburst, obscured the two central stars from direct observation.

Supernova Dreams Dashed

For years, V445 Puppis was considered a prime candidate to become a Type Ia supernova — the class of stellar explosions used as "standard candles" to measure cosmic distances and study the accelerating expansion of the universe driven by dark energy.

The white dwarf in the system was estimated to have a mass near the critical Chandrasekhar limit of approximately 1.4 solar masses — the threshold, named after Indian-American astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, above which a white dwarf becomes unstable and detonates.

"Whether V445 Puppis will eventually explode as a supernova, or if the current nova outburst has pre-empted that pathway by ejecting too much matter back into space is still unclear. But we have here a pretty good suspect for a future Type Ia supernova!"

— Patrick Woudt, University of Cape Town

That optimism, however, was overturned in December 2024. A comprehensive study by Bradley Schaefer of Louisiana State University, published on arXiv, determined that V445 Puppis ejected far more mass during its eruption than it had accumulated — meaning the white dwarf is losing mass with each eruption cycle, not gaining it. The orbital period analysis revealed the system's period shifted by 935 parts per million after the 2000 eruption, indicating a massive ejection well above 0.001 solar masses.

Schaefer also surveyed 136 normal Type Ia supernova remnants and found zero evidence of a giant or sub-giant companion star in any of them — an independent proof that helium novae like V445 Puppis are not supernova progenitors.

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

The research is deeply connected to the legacy of Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, who fled colonial India for Cambridge in 1930 and later became one of the 20th century's most influential astrophysicists. His eponymous mass limit remains central to understanding stellar death and cosmic expansion — the very questions V445 Puppis was once thought to help answer.

What's Next

V445 Puppis remains a one-of-a-kind laboratory. The companion star's orbital period of approximately 1.87 days, the unprecedented dust production — described as "dustier than a thousand novae" in a 2023 study published in the Astrophysical Journal Letters — and the still-obscured central binary all present ongoing research opportunities.

As the dust shell slowly thins, astronomers hope to directly observe the white dwarf and its companion for the first time. "We need to wait for that to become visible when the shell thins," Steeghs told Scientific American. "Because it's the first time we've seen a helium nova, there is no real benchmark."

The system may never explode as a supernova, but its cosmic bullets — still racing outward at 30 million km/h — continue to offer a unique window into the violent physics of stellar cannibalisation.
